title: DNS Extensions to Support IP Version 6
summary: Defines the changes to DNS to support IPv6 hosts. It adds the AAAA resource record type for storing an IPv6 address, a domain for looking up names from IPv6 addresses, and updated definitions of existing query types that return addresses. It is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The address book of the internet needs an entry type for the new long addresses. This memo creates it, along with a way to look up a name from an address.

questions: how do i do an ipv6 reverse dns lookup
subtitle: The AAAA record and IP6.ARPA domain that let DNS store and look up IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: DNS address queries were assumed by applications to return only 32-bit IPv4 addresses, so IPv6 addresses could not easily be stored in DNS.
tldr.mechanism: A new AAAA record type (type 28) holds one 128-bit IPv6 address, the IP6.ARPA domain maps an address back to a name, and NS, SRV and MX queries now add both A and AAAA records to the additional section.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard that combines and obsoletes RFC 1886 and RFC 3152, mainly by replacing the IP6.INT domain with IP6.ARPA.

facts.label: AAAA data
facts.value: One 128-bit IPv6 address, network byte order

today: RFC 3596 is an Internet Standard published in October 2003. It obsoletes RFC 1886 and RFC 3152, and the unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why DNS Needed Extending
sections.content:
The way DNS stores Internet addresses could not easily be extended to hold IPv6 addresses, because applications assume that address queries return 32-bit IPv4 addresses only. RFC 3596 defines three extensions: a resource record type that maps a name to an IPv6 address, a domain for lookups based on address, and a redefinition of existing queries that fill in the additional section.

The changes are designed to be compatible with existing software, and IPv4 support is kept. The IP version used to send a query is independent of the version of the records asked for, so IPv4 transport can be used to query IPv6 records and the other way round.
sections.plainLanguage: The old phone book only knew short numbers. Instead of throwing it away, the memo adds a new kind of entry next to the old ones.

sections.title: The AAAA Record Type
sections.content:
The AAAA resource record type is specific to the Internet class and stores a single IPv6 address. IANA assigned it the type value 28 (decimal). The 128-bit address is placed in the data portion in network byte order, high-order byte first.

A host that has more than one IPv6 address MUST have more than one AAAA record. In a master database file, the data is written as the textual form of an IPv6 address defined in RFC 3513.
sections.plainLanguage: An AAAA record is one line in the phone book with a name and one long number. A person with three numbers gets three lines.

sections.title: AAAA Queries
sections.content: An AAAA query for a domain name in the Internet class returns all the AAAA resource records for that name in the answer section of the response. A type AAAA query does not trigger additional section processing.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask for a name's long numbers and you get every long number listed for it. The answer does not come with extra pages of other information.

sections.title: The IP6.ARPA Reverse Domain
sections.content:
A special domain, rooted at IP6.ARPA, is defined to look up a record given an IPv6 address. Its intent is to map an address to a host name, though it may be used for other purposes as well.

An address becomes a name in this domain as a sequence of nibbles (four-bit values) separated by dots, ending with the suffix .IP6.ARPA. The nibbles are in reverse order, with the low-order nibble first, and each one is written as a hexadecimal digit. For the address 4321:0:1:2:3:4:567:89ab the reverse lookup name is the 32 nibbles shown in the figure below, followed by IP6.ARPA.
sections.plainLanguage: To find a name from a number, you write the number backwards, one digit at a time with dots between, then add a special ending. It is like reading a street address from the house number outwards.

sections.title: Changes to Existing Query Types
sections.content:
Queries that already add type A records to the additional section must now add AAAA records too. The RFC names three: name server (NS), location of services (SRV) and mail exchange (MX).

A name server therefore MUST add any relevant IPv4 addresses and any relevant IPv6 addresses it has locally to the additional section when it answers one of these queries.
sections.plainLanguage: When the phone book tells you which post office or mail server to use, it now also slips in that place's new long numbers, not just the short ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Any information obtained from DNS must be regarded as unsafe unless the techniques of RFC 2535 (DNS Security Extensions) or RFC 2845 (TSIG) are used. The AAAA record and the IP6.ARPA domain do not change how those techniques are used.

The RFC says it is not believed to cause any new security problems, nor to solve any existing ones. It also states that no IANA assignments are needed.
sections.plainLanguage: An answer from the phone book can be wrong unless it is signed. The new entries do not make that better or worse.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1886
sections.content:
RFC 3596 combines RFC 1886 and the changes made to it by RFC 3152, and obsoletes both. The main change is replacing the IP6.INT domain with IP6.ARPA.

Other changes: SRV is mentioned among the query types in Section 3, security considerations and IANA considerations sections were added, the references were updated, and the abstract and table of contents were added or updated.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a tidied-up version of an older memo. The biggest change is a new ending for the backwards lookup names.

items.title: AAAA record
items.text: Maps a domain name to an IPv6 address.

items.title: IP6.ARPA domain
items.text: Supports lookups based on an IPv6 address.

items.title: Additional section
items.text: NS, SRV and MX queries now include both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.
